heading: Are neurons polysemantic because features compete for limited capacity?
definition: neurons are polysemantic because features compete for limited capacity (important features get dedicated dimensions, others share).
summary: Independent toy-model studies confirm that, with the right sparsity and importance, important features get their own dimensions while the rest share dimensions. Capacity shortage as the general explanation is contested: polysemanticity also appears in networks with more neurons than features, and language-model evidence is mostly indirect, as in a Gemma distillation study where which features are kept depends on capacity but there is limited evidence that features share dimensions.

suggested_status.by_scale: Toy: R2 for conditional capacity allocation, C for the unqualified causal explanation. <1B: ? for full V2, with indirect specialization evidence. 1-10B: ? for full V2, with controlled distillation evidence for capacity-dependent retention. 10-100B: ? for full V2, with within-family specialization evidence. >100B: no identified counted coverage.
suggested_status.reason: Conditional toy allocation has an independent test in arXiv:2210.01892#r1 and arXiv:2210.01892#r4. But arXiv:2504.08842#r1 (8 pairwise-AND clauses on 16 hidden neurons) challenges capacity shortage as a necessary explanation for polysemanticity, and the checker confirms that challenges verdict. Gemma distillation establishes capacity-dependent retention, while its sharing evidence is limited (arXiv:2610.24521#r2, arXiv:2610.24521#r4, arXiv:2610.24521#r9). Natural-LLM scaling evidence remains indirect (arXiv:2505.17260#r2, arXiv:2505.17260#r6). The checker says arXiv:2505.17260's limits_scope verdict on similar-size models from different families (arXiv:2505.17260#r1) should be none; the level does not rest on that verdict. counts: versions.V2.verdicts.supports.studies=19; versions.V2.verdicts.limits_scope.studies=14; versions.V2.verdicts.challenges.studies=1. These are script counts made before the checks, so they still include the disputed verdict. Scale coverage follows versions.V2.studies_by_size, whose not-stated metadata prevent a complete scale assessment. C applies to the broad wording; it does not negate conditional capacity-allocation results.
suggested_status.open_questions: A matched natural-LLM experiment varying width and feature importance while measuring neuron-level sharing, dedicated allocation and dropping would strengthen the full causal account. Distinguishing capacity-driven sharing from incidental polysemanticity and showing when important features receive dedicated dimensions would determine whether a narrower statement merits R2 across real-model scales. C rests on the single challenges verdict (arXiv:2504.08842). If the spare-width polysemanticity proved absent under other training settings, or a narrower wording made capacity a sufficient rather than the necessary cause, the conditional toy R2 would be the remaining level.

source.title: Toy Models of Superposition
source.authors: Nelson Elhage; Tristan Hume; Catherine Olsson; Nicholas Schiefer; T. Henighan; S. Kravec; Zac Hatfield-Dodds; R. Lasenby; Dawn Drain; Carol Chen; R. Grosse; Sam McCandlish; J. Kaplan; D. Amodei; M. Wattenberg; Chris Olah

original_result.setup: They trained small ReLU toy models, varying feature sparsity and the relative importance of an extra feature from 0.1 to 10.
original_result.result: Whether a feature was ignored, given its own dimension or shared in superposition changed in phase transitions with sparsity and importance, and superposition needed sparsity. In a model computing absolute value, intermediate sparsity left some neurons pure and others highly polysemantic, and the neurons for the most important features tended to be monosemantic.
original_result.interpretation: This is the displayed original-result block, not a guarantee that the original tested every part of this claim.

sources.headline: Wider toy layers had more monosemantic neurons; polysemanticity rose as features per input approached the dimension.
Important features got full capacity, unimportant ones were ignored, intermediate ones shared.
A compressed Tracr-compiled transformer mostly kept critical variables in dedicated dimensions; less important sparse features shared.
Adding neurons while holding parameter count fixed raised feature capacity and reduced cosine similarity between neurons.
Neuron coverage of board-state properties in chess transformers rose as MLP width increased.
In toy mixture-of-experts models, adding experts kept a less important feature; too little capacity dropped it.
Shared feature coverage in toy autoencoders rose with neuron count.
Neuron specialization rose with model size, and frequent concepts got more specialized neurons.
Fixed-width Boolean MLPs hit a packing limit, and errors tracked clauses lacking codes.
Narrower distilled students had a matching neuron for fewer teacher neurons, favoring those with large activations.
Under a fourth-power (L4) loss, each neuron in a width bottleneck was shared by 10–12 features.
More frequent features received more effective dimensions under limited width.
Rosetta neurons (units matched across models) grew more selective with scale; other neurons did not.
A compressed dense student mixed many teacher neurons, with co-occurring features sharing regions.
Polysemanticity rose with sparsity, and the least important features were ignored.
When the most important feature was least sparse (most frequent), important features got dedicated dimensions.
Toy models favored higher-importance features and dropped low-importance ones.
With spare capacity, each neuron handled at most one feature; with limited capacity, neurons shared features.
With capacity allocated optimally, features shared dimensions when returns from extra capacity diminished.
Polysemantic basins appeared in wide layers, depending on training path rather than capacity.
With 6 features in 3 dimensions, features far more important than the rest were still superposed.
Polysemanticity arose in toy autoencoders without any capacity shortage.
On 12- or 32-literal Boolean formulas, adding neurons did not clearly reduce cosine similarity between neurons.
In toy mixture-of-experts models, which features got low superposition depended on router initialization, not only importance.
Specialization varied widely among similar-sized LLMs, tracking release date and accuracy.
In a 2560-neuron student, only 7% of teacher neurons lacked a matching neuron yet were shared.
Under L2 loss, the same width bottleneck gave features dedicated neurons or dropped them; none shared.
Competition took the form of discarded features and graded sharing, not dedicated dimensions.
In DINOv3, Rosetta neuron counts (units matched across models) showed no clear or monotonic scaling trend.
Dense OLMo-7B was still more polysemantic than mixture-of-experts OLMoE despite 7x more active parameters.
Polysemanticity arose in a toy setting with no capacity shortage.
When the most important feature was most sparse (least frequent), no feature got a dedicated dimension.
Toy MLPs with more neurons than features still became polysemantic.
With 16 neurons for 8 pairwise ANDs of inputs, networks still had polysemantic neurons.

wording_issues.issue: As an unqualified causal explanation, this rules out alternatives that have been observed. A two-layer MLP on a Boolean task has polysemantic neurons for 8 pairwise-AND clauses with 16 hidden neurons. That is a counterexample to capacity shortage as a necessary explanation. For ℓ1-regularized tied-weight autoencoders with m ≥ n, an analytic estimate gives an expected benign-collision count of n(n−1)/(4m), approximately n²/(4m). This is a derivation, not a measurement on a trained model. Experiments show a Θ(n²/m) trend. Separately, in continuous-valued feature-decoder and absolute-value tasks (active feature amplitudes uniform on [0,1]), polysemantic solutions occur even with enough nonlinear-layer width. There, monosemanticity depends on learning rate, bias initialization and bias decay. These results leave capacity competition possible as one cause. They do not establish it as the mechanism or as the only cause.

Dedicated allocation depends on the setting. In the Anthropic model, much more important features can stay superposed at 6 features in 3 dimensions. At 6 in 5, high-importance superposition does not persist. With non-uniform sparsity, Case 1 (most important feature least sparse) gives the more important features dedicated dimensions. Case 2 (most important feature most sparse) keeps shared representations with no dedicated dimension at any importance. In large sparse toy models (n=10000; unequal-frequency condition m=1000, ϵp=0.2), higher firing probability raises leverage score and bias and lowers norm. This is graded allocation, not dedicated dimensions for important features. The leverage-score comparisons cover only full-representation settings, where scores stay centred near m/n. The participation ratio r/m>1 at every tested width shows superposition in aggregate. It cannot show that no individual feature has a dedicated dimension.

Less-important or unretained features can be dropped. Under L2 computation training, the bottleneck yields dedicated handling and dropping without sharing. Gemma distillation provides limited evidence that unmatched teacher neurons survive through shared representations.

Several results bearing on V2 do not measure neurons. Tracr compression concerns residual-stream variables. In large sparse toy models, the firing-frequency result is graded leverage-score allocation. Dedicated dimensions and neuron polysemanticity are not shown there. Conditional-importance toy models measure feature retention without a privileged neuron basis. In the synthetic MoEs, 'monosemantic' means reduced superposition, not alignment to individual neurons. None of these measurements directly establishes neuron-level polysemanticity.

The statement does not say which capacity is limited, and different measures give different results. In Boolean DNF networks with 8 initial dense neurons, splitting neurons at a fixed non-zero parameter count raises measured feature capacity. In the OLMo family, with total parameters controlled, OLMoE-1B-7B gives cleaner single-neuron probed concept representations than OLMo-7B, although the dense model has 7× more active parameters per token. The authors attribute this mainly to sparse routing. Routing is not manipulated on its own, and feature competition is not measured, so this is an association. Among similarly sized open LLMs (about 6–8B), parameter specialization varies and is associated with SpecWiki accuracy and release date. Capacity and training history are not manipulated separately. None of these comparisons measures importance-dependent allocation.

method_sensitivity.factor: Feature importance, sparsity and firing frequency
method_sensitivity.what: In 5-feature ReLU output toy models, Case 1 (most important feature least sparse) gives more-important features dedicated dimensions while less-important ones share; in Case 2 (most important feature most sparse) all represented features stay in superposition and the important feature gets no dedicated dimension. These are qualitative results without numbers. In the n=10000 Anthropic toy model (mean active features 10, ϵp=0.2, widths including m=1000), higher firing probability increases leverage score and bias and decreases norm. This is graded allocation in a fully represented condition, with leverage scores staying near m/n, not dedicated dimensions. In toy models without a privileged neuron basis, conditional and fixed importance both qualitatively prioritize features with higher average importance.

The Anthropic model retains high-importance superposition in the 6-in-3 setting but not in 6-in-5. Its allocation differs from the quadratic computation model. Dedicated versus shared allocation therefore depends on the architecture and bottleneck ratio.

method_sensitivity.factor: Learning rate, bias initialization and training path
method_sensitivity.what: Wide feature decoders achieve similar loss with very different neuron monosemanticity across learning rates and bias settings. Wide absolute-value models also enter polysemantic basins despite sufficient neuron count. The toy replication separately reports sensitivity to bias initialization.
With the same computation bottleneck, L4 training produces overlapping feature codewords, while L2 training yields dedicated handling of half the features and drops the rest.

In synthetic MoE autoencoders (n=20 features, feature sparsity S=0.1, exponentially decreasing importance), which features get low-superposition representations depends on router initialization as well as importance. With ordered or random k-hot initialization, experts give low-superposition representations to the most important features among those initially routed to them. With ordered k-hot, the other experts do not monosemantically represent the five most important features outside their initial assignments; this does not show those features are ignored. Under uniform importance, initially occupied features have mean superposition scores 1.03 standard deviations below their expert's average. 'Monosemantic' here means less superposition, not alignment with individual neurons.

Narrower Gemma students preserve fewer dedicated teacher matches and increasingly favor high-energy teacher neurons. Wider toy feature decoders have more monosemantic neurons. Chess-model neuron coverage increases both when residual width and when the MLP expansion factor increase, with the scaling method affecting coverage.

method_sensitivity.factor: Selectivity proxy, judge input and model (Rosetta counts)
method_sensitivity.what: Rosetta language selectivity uses output-weight alignment to vocabulary embeddings rather than direct feature geometry. Vision monosemanticity rates decrease when more top-activating images are supplied to the VLM judge, while the Rosetta/non-Rosetta gap remains. Absolute judged rates depend on this setting. Rosetta-neuron counts also depend on the model: in DINOv3 they lack a clear monotonic scaling trend, unlike DINOv2 (Appendix I.1, Figure 38; text only, no pack row). The authors suggest dependence on interacting data, architecture, optimization and training objective; DINOv3's constraints on intermediate representations are a hypothesized cause. This limits the study's own Rosetta-count scaling law rather than V2's allocation effect; no DINOv3 importance-ranked allocation or selectivity result is reported.

method_sensitivity.factor: Concept popularity (frequency proxy) and model training history
method_sensitivity.what: In LLaMA2-7B and Qwen2-7B (base), parameter specialization score (PSS) decreases as concept popularity decreases across high, medium and low popularity groups, under concept-specific MLP-vector masking with multiple-choice evaluation. Popularity is a Wikipedia page-view proxy for pretraining frequency, not an independently manipulated importance variable, and accuracy also falls with popularity. The source names the second model inconsistently as Qwen2-7B and Qwen2.5-7B. Separately, across 20 open-source LLMs (§4.2, Figure 2), PSS correlates with SpecWiki multiple-choice performance (Pearson R=0.92, p=1.41e-08; Spearman 0.93, p=4.87e-09). Among similarly sized models (about 6–8B), PSS differs and is associated with accuracy and release date. This is a cross-model association: capacity and training history are not independently manipulated, and the text gives no numeric size for the variation.

method_sensitivity.factor: Routing sparsity (trained MoE vs dense LLMs)
method_sensitivity.what: In the OLMo family, OLMoE-1B-7B outperforms dense OLMo-7B on k=1 sparse logistic-regression probes. The measure is best-layer F1, mean over 58 concepts (part-of-speech, LaTeX, code, natural language). For the MoE, the best expert is chosen and data are filtered to tokens routed to it. OLMo-7B has 7× more active parameters per token, and total parameter counts are matched. Exact F1 values are figure-only, with 95% confidence intervals. The authors attribute the difference mainly to sparse routing. Routing is not independently manipulated, so this is an association. Feature competition and importance-ranked capacity allocation are not measured, and the checker reads r1 and r3 as cannot_determine for V2. This is a setting that changes probed single-neuron polysemanticity, not a test of the capacity account.
